utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. On this Thursday I would like to greet all the parties who are present. I would like to greet Mr. Scott, the counsel for the Defence, as well as anybody inside this courtroom and outside the courtroom. We are now going to finish the hearing of this witness, and contrary to what was said after erroneous calculations, it would seem that Mr. Praljak has two hours and not two hours and 20 minutes, as we thought, since he gave back to Ms. Nozica 20 minutes, which means that he has two hours, but that is sufficient enough, I believe. So, Mr. Kovacic, how are things going to look today? Are you going to begin and then Mr. Praljak will intervene with regard to military questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, and bearing in mind your recent ruling, I should like to ask your indulgence for Mr. Praljak to start first, and I think he'll cover everything since the areas that I had in mind have already been covered, and he has justified reasons for conducting the cross-examination. As you well know, the witness spoke about the fact that they met several times in persons, and there are a number of significant facts related to the events in which Praljak was involved himself personally, and there are various military and technical matters that the witness mentioned indirectly, and Mr. Praljak would like additional information. So that is why I would like to leave the cross-examination to Mr. Praljak and, if necessary, I can ask a few questions after that to round it off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, Your Honours, and all those in the courtroom. Again, just so the record is clear, and we'll just say this -- I'll I won't make this same objection today in the interest of everyone saving time, but, just for the record, the Prosecution continues to object to this mode of presentation. It appears to the Prosecution, with all respect, that there is simply no limits whatsoever on Mr. Praljak's participation in questioning or in other comments in the courtroom. Despite the fact that there's been some apparent reference or talk about there being some limitation, there does not appear to the Prosecution to be any limitation whatsoever. Any topic is fair game, any comment that Mr. Praljak wants to make is fair game. It's not limited to technical matters, and we simply note our continuing objection to this procedure. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your objection is noted, but, as the Chamber stated, the accused may intervene when he is personally concerned, since he met the witness, he assisted to various meetings, which is the case in this particular case, since is the witness did meet Mr. Praljak. And whenever there are technical questions to be dealt with, the accused who is an expert in that matter can intervene because he knows the matter better than his lawyer. So, Mr. Praljak, you've heard my intervention. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just like to say something with respect to time. I wasn't given time from Ms. Nozica. You gave, out of your benevolence, 15 minutes to Ms. Nozica, so I have two hours and 20 minutes according to my calculations. That's one point. And secondly -- may I be allowed to finish. And we're dealing with questions that I took part in, Offensive 93, the participation of the Croatian army, the brigade questions, and so on and so forth. So Mr. Petkovic and I have information about questions of this nature, and they are technical ones, precise questions, and I have been mentioned on a number of occasions in this connection. So I don't see why I would not be able to ask these questions, and the Prosecution did touch upon technical issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before handing the floor to Mr. Scott, with regard to the 15 or 20 minutes, yesterday I was told that during the cross-examination at one point Ms. Nozica stated that the Defence of Mr. Praljak could give her 15 or 20 minutes. I don't know any more. We would have to read the transcript. Then she turned towards Mr. Praljak, and at that point there was tacit agreement and an agreement was concluded. Maybe I'm mistaken. Ms. Nozica, is that what happened? We're not going to, of course, listen to the video again. Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I also understood it that the Trial Chamber allowed me to complete my cross-examination, and Mr. Praljak didn't give me any of his time. All I said was that, as we have 15 minutes left, may the Trial Chamber -- will the Trial Chamber allow me to complete my cross-examination today before Mr. Praljak begins. I did not ask for time from Mr. Praljak, nor did I get time from Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I don't want to waste time, but there is a certain point to this. I think there's some matter of principle in this. I'm really quite surprised to hear counsel say that. It was quite clear to me. My observations in the courtroom were exactly as the President's. At the time when the Trial Chamber reminded counsel for Mr. Stojic that time was up, counsel turned to Mr. Praljak asking for more time. Mr. Praljak nodded, gave the indication that he was willing to give up some time to her, and that's what happened. That's exactly what I saw in the courtroom. Really, again, I'm very surprised to hear to the contrary. 20 minutes is 20 minutes. It's not going to be the end of this case either way, but, Your Honour, I mean, time always seems to expand on and on without being controlled in any meaningful way when it comes to the Defence side of the case. I'm sorry to say that, but 20 minutes was given up and I don't think this 20 minutes has to come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just proceed and perhaps, if there's need for -- based on relevancy, then the Bench can obviously reconsider its position. I think we're wasting time by having this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's not a waste of time unless -- unless the time limits don't matter. Time limits are put on the Prosecution all the time, and we don't turn to another counsel and say, Can we have 20 more minutes from somebody else, and that's clearly what happened yesterday. And out of fairness and out of some sort of some courtroom decorum, some rules should be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have found the place in the transcript. It's page 100, line 23, I think, and it was a bit ambivalent indeed. Ms. Nozica turned around and said, "Well, my time's up." If Mr. Praljak would like to continue. And then there was sort of a silence which he understood as being allowed, and the Presiding Judge in fact let her go on, and I think it is defendable to say that this was a gift out of the endless generosity of the Chamber. So I just want the Defence teams to realise how extremely generous we are, and I have a good understanding for the Prosecution thinking that we are being too generous. But in this specific case, I think, as there is some ambivalence indeed, I think we assume that we take that on ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Praljak, you have two hours and 20 minutes. Go ahead, please. We've already lost 10 minutes on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Watkins.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm happy to see you again. I'd like to start off with documents for my first question. Now, while you were in Central Bosnia or later on in Mostar, ever heard had of an operation called Neretva 93?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you now look at the documents. 3D 00931 is the first one, please. 3D 00931. It is a document dated the 28th of August, 1993, and they are conclusions and tasks from a consultation of the senior offices of the Main Staff army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in Zenica on the 21st and 22nd of August, 1993. Do you have that, sir? Conclusions and tasks adopted at the meeting of senior officers and corps commanders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document. I'm just seeing if there's an English version of it. Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at who was present from the Supreme Command Main Staff. Take a look at the names and the names of those present from the corps, and then I'm going to ask you this: You were there for quite a long time. Now, the names of these commanders from the Main Staff, the Supreme Command and Corps, was there anybody there who wasn't a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember meeting one military commander who wasn't a Muslim, but I -- I don't see his name here and I can't recall it. So from what I can see here, I would say that these are all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us take a look at the conclusions, and conclusion number 1 first. It says that the war was waged for 17 months against the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor and the former JNA, and that it was -- that's how it was, and then it says, "a war imposed by the extremist portion of the HVO is in fact a stab in the back to the BH army." So they claim that the HVO stabbed them in the back. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now take a look at point 2,"The goals and objectives of our army remain the fight for a Bosnia-Herzegovina state and a uniform state within the recognised borders." Now, when it says "united" here, and if borders are mentioned, then it denotes a political project of one man, one vote. Did you know these objectives, to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- an integral state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Where does it say in one man, one vote? It does not say in the official translation here, unified or something. It says "indivisible," and that's not quite the same. Perhaps we need the assistance of the interpreters. It's certainly not unitarian. It's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Maybe there's a translation error. Could you please tell us in your language the word in B/C/S, because indivisible is one thing and to unify is another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] United.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 2, "the goals of our army's fight remain the same, a struggle for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, united --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, interpreter's note, "integrated."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "-- and within recognised borders." Now, if in the sentence it says, "within recognised borders," then the word "jadinstre no [phoen]," in the Croatian language means precisely what I'm asking the witness. "Jadinstre no," "united," in the political sense means one man, one vote. Now I'm asking the witness whether he knew of this position taken by the BH army. That's not there, but there's no reason to write that. There's no need to use the word "jadinstre no--"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Meaning "united" or "integrated," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and within recognised borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are interpreting this, this way, but please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that will the term "united," a united Bosnia-Herzegovina army, was being prepared by a political goal of one man, one vote? Just say yes or no, if you know that or not, because I have a lot of documents to get through.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the Bosnian army's position is, as it is translated in paragraph 2, that they wished to retain the state of Bosnia which had been recognised, Bosnia and Herzegovina, indivisible within its recognised borders. I can't contribute to the debate about united. It was very clear: They wanted to maintain what the international community had recognised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Although both in the Bosnian language and Croatian language, the word "cjelovita [phoen]," "integral," is appropriate. And now look at point 3: "The war for territories will continue even if peace on the basis of the Geneva agreement is reached." What do you know about that, their position that they would continue the war even if peace were achieved on the basis of the Geneva Convention -- agreement? And then it says the continuing war will be aimed against both types of Fascism, Serbian-Montenegrin and Croatian. What do you know about their position according to which Fascism is mentioned, Serbian-Montenegrin and Croatian and that both have been equated in that sentence there in their position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it was regularly expressed to us by the armija forces that they felt that the Serbs who they were fighting against were of fascist in nature and also the Croatian HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll skip over certain points where they say how things developed on a military level, but let us focus on paragraph 8 first and then 9. It says that, "the purchase of weapons, ammunition and military equipment, despite complicated delivery across the aggressor's territory, may be effected through the involvement of all available factors and methods, from friends to enemies, from patriots to war profiteers, and traitors from the aggressor's armed units." Now Mr. Watkins, I'm asking you the following: You're a soldier. When you were seeing that the BH army had weapons, did you see them have tanks, mortars, helicopters? Did you see all that? Did you observe all that, that they had those weapons?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed that they had mortars and helicopters. I don't remember seeing any tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you see the artillery pieces, any artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only saw mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please, when as a soldier you saw all this and were wondering where they were firing from, and -- did you wonder where the weapons came from and what enemy territories were they referring to, the Serbs, the Croats, Herceg-Bosna? Did you wonder about all these things?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were very interested to understand trade in weapons and indeed other elements, and over the period of my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina I came across some extraordinary alliances and seemingly unlikely trading deals. I would evidence myself at a meeting where Muslims were meeting Serbs in the town of Turbe to the north of Travnik where a deal was being done, supply of steel by the Muslims in return for humanitarian aid, and I think I've already given some indications previously of trade between Croat forces and Serb forces, and there were some extremely interesting relationships in other areas of Bosnia, such as the Bihac pocket where Fikret Abdic was striking deals with anyone. It was a case, as stated here. I think quite interestingly, they were prepared to deal with anyone and anything -- anybody, to get the weapons they felt they needed to survive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. Now take a look at paragraph 11, where it says that, "the organs of state authority"-- paragraph 11, please -- "of the BH army during the time that an armed conflict was going on were at a divergence with the general guidelines for an armed struggle. State authority was only partially placed in the function of war, which had as a result an inadequate logistical support for the armed forces." So from that -- those consultations would you agree that the BH army, according to your information, not only thought that regardless of the political agreement in Geneva that the war would continue but that it was dissatisfied with its political authorities?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw conclusion from paragraph 11, which is similar to the situation I described. Certain armija Muslim forces were quite distance physically and in terms of communication from Sarajevo, and certainly I think there were elements of sort of independent thought and action.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, if we look at tasks, chapter 2 and point 5, it says: "The combat morale of soldiers and units shall be built up on patriotism and the traditions of the Bosnian nation and heroic examples of combatants and units from this war." The Bosnian nation, is that Croats, Serbs, or just Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we could draw any specific conclusion. It could be the state we've described earlier of a nation of all those constituent groups. Equally I agree that one could interpret, if you chose to, that it was very specifically Muslim but it's ambiguous as it's translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Now next document, 3D 00932, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is dated the 7th of September. Let me first ask you whether you know the name at the bottom, Arif Pasalic. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of 4th Corps based in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you see that here in point 2, last paragraph, he said -- he says the following: "As agreed, one or two companies of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the BH army are supposed to be September to the zone of the 4th Corps," et cetera. And in paragraph 4 he goes on to enumerate the units to be attached to Operative Group North 2, or Cijevevet [phoen] 2 for the full implementation of tasks. And in order to clear the enemy forces in the Neretva River valley, he proposes that a dominant feature of attack be in the HVO forces in the area of Cordina Kula and Jedrenje. Do you consider that from this we can see that mop-up operation of HVO is being planned in the Neretva river valley? Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now the next document 3D 00933, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a document dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is something which -- which strikes me in the point 4. Mr. Pasalic writes "I propose," and that strikes me as a very unmilitary language. He proposed to whom, and who is going to decide? Perhaps you could enlighten us to -- on that. Perhaps it is again a matter of translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right. I'm going to present documents and then we'll go into that. This operation, Neretva 93, it was Sefer Halilovic who commanded the operation, the chief at the time. We'll come to that very -- later on, and he is proposing -- the proposal is made to Sefer Halilovic. So next document, 3D 00393.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander who took on from Arif Pasalic, Budakovic, signed his name as Tetak, that that was his nickname? He was also known as Tetak, or "uncle," in translation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Once again, it is sent to Sefer Halilovic, the forward command post, Sefer Halilovic, and Zulfikar Alipasic [as interpreted], and it says, "20 soldiers from," et cetera, et cetera. "Zulfikar unit will attack towards the hills from the direction of Solakovac-Jedrinje towards you. I have assigned the task for Karadza to invest all efforts to use artillery fire from the hill in the Ustasha depths south of Vrdi," et cetera, et cetera. Now, Witness, is it clear from this that they are attacking and that they do have artillery weapons to fire into the opposite side's territory and depth? Is that what is clearly -- what clearly follows from this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does clearly suggest that an attack is being organised. I would just be careful about assuming that artillery is tube artillery, and I myself, as an artillery officer, have already in the course of the last few days used the word artillery when I might more specifically have meant mortars. So I think we just have to be quite careful about that. But it doesn't preclude the fact that this could be tube artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, we've already heard other witnesses here and documents about that but we'll see. Let's look at document 3D 00931. It's dated 5 September 1993, again addressed to Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the main command of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction, Your Honours. This should be document 934.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I misread. 00934.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, why don't you give a stand to your client? It might be easier for him then to conduct his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Look at the members of the main command, Rifet, Damadje [phoen], and others. It says, "We received a reply from Vaho explaining that they will not be able to send any soldiers due to the recent developments. "Sefer, we need to find and pull out other soldiers from Sarajevo because we cannot do the job without a reserve of 200 soldiers." Is it clear from this that in the operation which is being prepared, and which is in fact under way, help is required from Sarajevo, units from outside are being pulled in? Is that obvious from this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, 3D 00935.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Dated 9 September, with a request for the minister of the interior, Bakir Alispahic to come to that area because he has a meeting with Mahmutcehajic. That's written by Sefer Halilovic. Do you know who Bakir Alispahic was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by reference to this document. He is the Minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Document 3D 00936, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Dated 13 September, security organ of the 6th Corps. We see from this that there is a 6th Corps, which some of your documents deny, and it says here: "Commander Musfet Cahic -- sorry, Nusret Sahic. Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It might help if I -- could you just orient me to where the name is on the page? Oh, sorry, right at the bottom. No, I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at the document. It says, "On the 10th of August, 1993, I was in Jablanica to check and assist the work of the subordinated unit, Jablanica military police company," et cetera. It says then: "While I was in the department for service, commander Djelmo Zenaid informed me that allegedly a genocide over Croatian population occurred in the town of Grabovica perpetrated by a person unknown from the ranks of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We immediately went to Grabovica and found out that in fact genocide did happen and that on that occasion around 20 civilians were slaughtered and killed." Have you heard about the crime in Grabovica that happened in September?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got down into Mostar, it was one of the issues that was raised, and I believe it was raised by Slobodan Bozic and also Mr. Prlic, and we were asked to carry out our own investigation. I don't remember us getting any detail. It is an interesting confession here that it has happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next document then, 3D 00937. It's a document dated 1st September, 1993, and as you will see at the bottom, "Rasim Delic, commander of the Supreme Command of the armed forces orders the establishment of the 6th Corps to include units such as Black Swans, Zulfikar silver fox, Akrepi, Muderiz," and others. It also deals with military issues, who was subordinated to whom. But at any rate, do you know that at this time the 6th Corps was set up and certain units were included?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Corps was, as you pointed out, something of a mystery to us. We have reported, and indeed I remember seeing yesterday one of our teams, Mike 1, talking to somebody, and we acknowledge he was talking to somebody from 6th Corps, but we couldn't establish where the boundaries were, and I do agree with you, Mr. Praljak, that somewhere I remember doing a sort of summary of calls, and we conclude that had 6th corps didn't exist, but -- so we were getting mixed messages on it. But this is pretty clear if this is an official document that it did exist with those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If there is a pause, Witness, we have before us an order. How do you know that the order was executed? You state this as if it -- as if this were evidence of the existence, and I read it as evidence of someone ordering this formation to be created.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very good point, Your Honour. I did -- the only assumption that I made was that this was an official document, but you're right, it's about an order that it should happen rather than it is formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. What matters more to me in this document -- in fact, let us look at 938. What matters more to me is the discrepancy between your knowledge - and of course you tried hard - about what happened on the ground and what you managed to include in your documents. Now, document 938, dated 7 September 1993, signed by Arif Pasalic, and you said you knew that he was commander of the 7th corps. And he orders certain units here pursuant to a previous order that we saw. The Supreme Command Staff issued an order pursuant to which the following units are placed under the command of the 4th Corps: Zulfikar, Muderiz, Akrepi, and silver fox. With a zone of responsibility, Operative Group North 2, north Jablanica south [as interpreted] excluding the hydro power station Salakovac. Do you know where that hydro power plant was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's to the north of Mostar on the river Neretva.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, 3D 00939. It's signed by Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the BH army, dated 6 September 1993. And it says, attaching certain maps: "With regard to previous 6 Corps unit's task and combat operations in the 4th Corps' zone of responsibility, and the engagement of the Zulfikar reconnaissance-sabotage brigade on the axis Vrdi village-Goranci village towards Mostar, the following units are resubordinated or seconded to this brigade, including certain artillery weapons, 120-millimetre mortars, two of them, one 105-millimetre howitzer and one 132-millimetre howitzer, two 76 millimetre B-1 cannon, and one 107-millimetre rocket launcher system." You see how the artillery was organised only on this axis. Do you believe that this was the only artillery in the possession of the BH army if they are employing all of this only on the Vrdi village axis? Was there any difference between what you were reporting and what existed in reality? You can give me a simple answer such as, "I wasn't aware of this," or --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to look at a map to comment about the access Vrdi, but the point with regards to the weapons system is, here is a statement of weapons, which I did not see, which it appears, if this is accurate, that they had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, let's be simple. I'm not claiming that you saw them. I'm just saying that on one single access of attack, and I'll show you Neretva 93 later, on just one axis of attack they have this artillery. You said you didn't see them. You said they only had 20-millimetre mortars. In the last paragraph, "On Neretva, regulate the time and the method of releasing water from the reservoir of the hydro power plant Salakovac, which is one of the crucial issues in executing the following tasks." Have you ever heard about using water from the reservoir to flood the lower field to achieve some of their combat tasks in that area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. Could I just return to this issue --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the access of attack and artillery? Artillery, of course, one of the flexibility of the weapon is that it is able to engage on many fronts or several fronts from a single position because --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Watkins, we will see on the map where Vrdi village is and where other BH army units are elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We cannot assume that somebody was going to haul artillery from Vrdi village. We just saw that it was employed on one axis, and as for other axes, we will see that from other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief interruption. We have two 120-millimetre mortar, one of the 105, two of 76, one rocket launcher. Here we have a list of weapons. With that list, can you tell us if a military unit that would have these weapons, would that unit have very important or high firepower, a medium firepower? What is your assessment, because you are an artillery officer. What we see here on this document, is that the sign of very high artillery fire capacity? What is your assessment until.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say this is a significant gathering of artillery in terms of the scale of warfare in Bosnia. It wouldn't equate to any Western army in terms of very much artillery, but in these circumstances it is a collection of artillery. And the point I was making with General Praljak, although General Praljak and myself and one or two others here understand the use of artillery, artillery is an asset which is usually held at a high level of command, and it is allocated to units as they need it. And because of its range, it can be in such a position to support several units at any one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a question. It is -- is it normal and usual to mix such a sample of all different kinds of cannons, in the broadest sense, to form mixed artillery units, or is this, rather, something which is -- looks as being scraped together here and there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the latter, Your Honour, because it is an interesting mix, and I think it's a case of what weapons did they have and, yes, to gather them together, it is not normal to have such a range, as you can imagine, logistically for an artillery battery or regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Document 3D 00940. We see actually from the previous document that it was resubordinated from the 4th Corps especially for this task, but it's written in the document. I cannot waste too much time on it though. Let's move on to document 3D 00940 [as interpreted] and then document 941.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 940 and 941.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 941. We'll skip 940, because it deals with similar things. Let's move on to 941. It's a report, actually, on an incident mentioned previously as the massacre in Grabovica. It's a large document, and on page 2 there is a passage in the middle of the page where it says: "The said situation in Grabovica is under control, and a contributing factor was that Ramiz Delalic executed his own soldier after this. Information about it is kept confidential to the extent possible, all with a view to completing the combat operation which is being prepared." So a combat operation is being prepared, and the information about the Grabovica incident is kept confidential. Is that written in the document, sir, and what do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just quickly looking at the document. I just want to check the question. Yes, a combat operation is being prepared and I just need to find where it says about keeping the information confidential. I couldn't find it while you were saying it but I'm not saying it isn't here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just below. It says: "Information is kept confidential to the extent possible." So they are not releasing any info about the investigation because that could disrupt preparations for an operation.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now have Exhibit 3D 00942? It was used in another case before this Tribunal against Sefer Halilovic. This is a book written by a journalist, Sefko Hodzic, called "A Sealed Envelope." Could we go quickly through the document to see -- this was published in Sarajevski List newspaper and Oslobodjenje, and it was regularly broadcast over Radio Sarajevo as a live broadcast of sorts of the Neretva 93 operation. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document entitled, "The Last Supper at Ark."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct. All my questions will be to the effect did you know about it, and if you didn't, then your reports would be seriously deficient. Saturday, 4 September 1993, and at the end of the paragraph it says: "Pasalic wrote that HVO is preparing an all-out attack on Mostar. Expected within seven days. Sefer says we'll attack them first. Units will be assembling on Sunday. Reconnaissance will be on Monday and Tuesday and Wednesday will be the attack. Third paragraph from the bottom it says: "Sefer ordered Karavelic therefore to go to Herzegovina --" sorry, "to send to Herzegovina the Delta brigade parts of the 9th and 10th mountain brigades." It says, "If you believe that the defence of Sarajevo will be damaged by this I take personal responsibility." So it is clear from this that he's weakening the defence of Sarajevo in order to conduct this operation in the Neretva River valley. Do you interpret this the same way that I do?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next page, please, the middle of the page. It says: "They returned to the Zulfikar unit base in Jablanica where Delic, commander of the BH army, arrived previously, as well as Vran, Bilajac Suljevic, Karic, Zuka. They held a meeting." And if it goes on to say, "All these units needed to be integrated and placed under the command of the Zulfikar unit in the Neretva operation." We see that that is the name of the operation they are preparing, Neretva. Do you see the same thing?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry, could you just orientate me on that page? I'm on page 2 -- no, sorry, 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "We returned to the base of the unit Zulfikar in Donja Jablanica."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, it's page 3 -- page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can find it on the screen, the court support. I have it in front of me now on the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we see a reference to this operation as Neretva; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page now. In your text it's page number -- just a minute. I'm skipping over a portion. Your page 3, last paragraph on that page. "We discussed battles and commanders. I asked Delic if he believed these negotiations on peace would really bring peace or were they simply ornaments of the war." And the next sentence reads: "I think they are merely decorative and the war will of course go on." Answer Delic: "It goes on. Negotiations are only hurting us, lower the troops' morale." Did you see this, namely that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina demonstrates through a number of documents that peace negotiations are in fact something they do not agree with? Could you please give me an answer? Is that correct? Do we see that from the documents you have before you and the ones we saw previously?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid after all the praise yesterday, when you start I'm not orientated on the page. I cannot see that. So I think to avoid me keep going back we need to establish carefully where you're starting. I am on page 3, according to my translation, but I don't see the words that you're relating to. If you can just point me on to the document then I'll be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Page 3, last paragraph, the bottom of the page. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, starting "The chief of Ark."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "We discussed also both battles and commanders. I asked Delic if he believed that these peace negotiations would really bring peace --"

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, General Praljak, I'm not able to follow that. I am on page 3, and the last paragraph does not start as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, can you please repeat the page number. 3D 25, what is the number after that? You see that at the bottom of the page we have various figures, various numbers, 482, 483. What page are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in e-court now. It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Praljak, I now have that. It's on my page 4, which is the cause of confusion. Or using the reference of the numbers at the end, 0483.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we were also talking about battles and commanders. I asked Delic if he believed that these peace negotiations were really going to bring peace or they were just war ornaments, and the reply is: "I reckon they are ornaments and that the war continues," he replies. "From negotiations we suffer damage only," Sefer added. "The morale of the fighters is dropping. "Sefer, and what you say: We will reach Ploce too. Delic, smiling, says to Sefer, alluding to the recent statement made by Sefer that our army was going to reach Ploce. Hat statement raised a huge outcry in the Croatian press. Sefer, also smiling, explained how that gaffe had occurred. 'I took the stage at a rally in Podrinjaca,' [phoen] he narrated to us. I was talking about how we were going to liberate every part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how our army was going to reach Bosnian borders, reach Neum ... that someone from the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot see the page any more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you hear such statements that they were going to go as far as the western borders, including Ploce in Croatia? And my first question is in fact: Is it clear to you from these documents and the previous ones that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not believe -- did not have any faith in the negotiations, that regardless of them the war was going to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this time. Number one, there's no foundation. There's no way that this witness can add evidentiary value to the mere -- once again we are back to reading documents. I expect Mr. Praljak can read books to the witness all day long and ask him whether he's ever seen the book or not. It doesn't add anything. The witness cannot speculate as to the motives or policy of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, Your Honour, specifically focused on this detail, the witness did mention some political statements with respect to Ploce, but what is even more important is that the witness quite obviously is very well-informed, and we heard his excellent testimony, and if we read out an assertion from a document or another source and he is asked whether that corresponds to what he knows about it, then I think this is an absolutely acceptable method employed by the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will myself deal with this problem. Witness -- you've stated your objection. What would you like to add? You stated that you did not agree. You were objecting, right? Is this what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could make a further comment in respect -- in response to counsel, I would very much appreciate it. Your Honour, the point, we could simply stand here all day and read from book -- there's -- endless books have been written on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we can put -- read out statements to the witness all day, and it just simply is not a proper way to proceed unless it is something that specifically involved the witness. I understand if there is a book that says -- if there's a book that gives an account and says On such-and-such a day, observer Watkins attended a meeting, and he can then comment on that and say, yes, in fact, I was at that meeting and all that, but this is just general material that can be put in front of the witness all day long from hundreds of books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just briefly in response, if I might be allowed to do so. The Prosecution brought in this witness. It selected the witness. It chose the topic of discussion for the witness, and the area of discussion is extremely broad. We have received excellent information from this witness at a very global level spanning more than one year, highly relevant information, and by that very fact, the fact that the Prosecution included this in its material opened the door to the Defence to go even broader in conformity with the rules and regulations and to present its lines of defence therein. So if the Prosecution has problems with the breadth of the cross-examination and in putting certain sources to the witness, then they must change their tactics and bring in witnesses that will just focus on little bits and pieces, and then we will be more succinct. But when they bring in such broad-based witnesses testifying about such a broad area then they have to take as much as they get from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were an observer of the European Union at the time, and you drafted many reports. We were able to notice that some paragraphs are entitled "Political," so you have knowledge in politics, we conclude. You've also stated that you were following the Vance-Owen Plan and the way it was progressing and implemented. Now, there is a book, and Mr. Praljak could read you paragraphs. Maybe he could have put a simple question to you. So there is a book in which we see that very important people from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina are indicating that they are preparing a military operation and that they would go almost to the borders of Croatia. The accused, Mr. Praljak, wanted to put the following question to you, and this could be an interesting question and could be relative. As an observer of the events that were taking place at the time, are you able to assess or analyse the situation and tell us that if on the one hand the parties who were on the ground are making agreements, cease-fire agreements, they're negotiating for peace, they're making statements, such statements, whereas in this document we see that they have the intention to go very far on a military plan. Isn't there a contradiction in terms here, a contradiction in things, if at the time as an observer you knew this book? If you had read this book, if you knew the contents of this book, what would you have said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think it is such a contradiction. Looking at this page and seeing the conversation, we see two senior armija discussing the extent of their military activity and the suggestion that the military thrust would be as far as Ploce. What is also, I think, clear from this statement is that Mr. Delic considers that he is rather being perhaps a little silly in making that statement and refers to how it happened. It is not uncommon that military personnel make statements, and sometimes their political masters then disagree or keep them in check. I think any military commander in this war at this time, be it HVO or armija, were planning actions to take territory, and so I'm not surprised that at the time that we have the Geneva discussions going on, we have military commanders planning activity and doubting their political masters. It is a very common thing that military, while they do obey or should obey their political masters, will always be questioning the wisdom and the likelihood of the success of the other strand of activity, i.e., the political negotiations. So we have political negotiations going on at Geneva, uncertainty here in the case of the armija forces as to whether that's going to be successful or not; meanwhile, they're prosecuting their element, which is either holding or taking more territory. And here, a statement that it will go as far as Ploce but then the commander saying that he hadn't sort of meant to but somebody shouted it out, and he in a, maybe a rush of blood to the head, said, "Yes, and Ploce too." But he's already -- the fact that he's indicated as smiling and so on, I think he thinks he knows that that was a step too far. Sir, I don't know whether that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all -- with great respect to this witness, who is indeed very knowledgeable and very articulate, but if you look at the answer we've just given, it's just a comment on what's been read in a book on meetings that he didn't attend, and "he said with a smile," so-and-so said with a smile, and all -- again, we can read these kind of material all day long. It does not add any evidentiary value for -- to do that, and plus, on a specific point of contradiction, if -- if there was specific material that contradicted something the witness said, then that should specifically be put to the witness and the particular material should be put to the witness, but, again, to go through books and then say we're putting this on for the purpose of contradicting the witness, I don't think it's improper -- I think it is not proper, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond, Your Honour. First of all, the Prosecution does this all the time with its documents, showing documents to witnesses where the witness did not generate the document, wasn't present at any meetings where the document was generated, and so on and so forth. So we've objected. The Trial Chamber has indicated that the Prosecution can go forward. So I don't see why the Prosecution now is making a fuss of this. Secondly, and more importantly, the Prosecution through this gentleman has elicited certain testimony. Also, the gentleman wrote certain reports because he was in the field at the time and had access to relevant information, although, as we established earlier, particularly in the cross-examination that I did, that the gentleman was labouring under a situation where he did not have access to all of the information. Now what General Praljak is doing is providing further information to the gentleman and asking him, based on his own experience both in the field and his background, and the gentleman has eight years in the British Army, so based on that, now he's being given an opportunity to have further information and to give further opinions as to what might have been happening. I think this is very relevant. I think this is a proper way of proceeding, and I see nothing that Mr. Praljak is doing that I would not do if I were granted the time to do this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you may proceed. The witness answered your question. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Your Honour, now why is this basic and the foundation? I want through witness, who was there and provided information, to show -- well, I showed him documents, and the book arguments -- the documents, and -- there was an offensive which went on for one month, and that's what it says in the book. So I have to ask why there's nothing about that in the report they compiled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, if you look at another excerpt, which begins on Friday the 10th of September, 1992, and it is entitled, "A Story Told by the Boys that Survived." Yes, I will find the page for reference. And we'll skip over the first three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page, what document number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of the document is the same, but I'm being told that there's no further translation because originally Mr. Praljak had not intended to go that far. So it does not exist in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But let me ask you this Sefer's words about our offensive are talked about a lot. Do you know whether the offensive existed or not? Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that Sefer said, referring to the offensive, that it is the largest BH army operation to date, and that if the offensive is successful it will completely change the strategic situation in the country and he also said that President Izetbegovic would have trump cards up his sleeve at the negotiations with that. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, these are two issues each time. First, you say, but without any foundation, that someone said something, then you ask the witness whether he knew. But we would first, I think, have to know whether in fact these statements have been made. This is a -- this book is hearsay, of course. It's just a journalist who says that he has heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that it said in the book that all those reports were broadcast over Radio Sarajevo and published in the paper Oslobodjenje. But I'll give up on the rest and just show the document about Neretva 93, and the document number is as follows 3D 00885. Let me repeat. 3D 00885 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look at it, and my first question is this: Do you know that the offensive lasted for a month, roughly a month, from the 12th of September, 1993, to, let's say, the 10th of October, 1993? Do you know about that? Yes, no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time I was in -- further up in Central Bosnia, so I wasn't aware of the timing specifically of the month.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, please, we know you were in Central Bosnia, but try and answer the question. Do you know about that offensive, and do you know that it lasted a few days under a month? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me two parts of a question, so yes or no wouldn't be adequate. Yes, I knew about the offensive. No, I did not know that it lasted a few days under a month.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that the offensive stretched from Makljen and the attack on Gornji Vakuf right up to the attack towards Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, and towards the south, from Mostar towards Blagaj, Capljina, et cetera? Is that something that you know about, that the front was 200 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of any BH army offensive against the Serbs before this date and after this date which would be even half as intensive in terms of manpower and unit involvement?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the large-scale fighting that took place in 1992 with armija and HVO together fighting the Serbs, if that's what you're drawing me towards. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, I wasn't thinking of that. I was just thinking of one BH army action, but let's move on. 3D 00945 is the next document I'd like us to look at. 3D 00945. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 17th of September, and take a look at the page and you'll see that Stjepan Siber was signing standing in for the commander, and he says deputy BH commander and look at the preamble. "Accepting the principles of the London conference and determined to cease hostilities and create conditions for peace," et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says, "The president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the so-called SR Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, the president -- President of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic, and the president of the so-called Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, signed a joint declaration in Geneva on the 16th of September, 1993. With a view to the realisation of that I hereby order that the units of the BH army should immediately and at the latest by the 18th of September at 12.00 noon cease all hostilities against paramilitary Serb aggressor formations in conformity with the agreement reached on the 30th of July. Does it follow clearly from this that they are establishing a truce, a cease-fire, ceasing hostilities against the Serbs, in the throes of what you're talking about, that is an attack on the HVO Neretva 93. So is this a document which says that conflicts with the Serbs are ceasing at the same time when all the documents, and unfortunately we would need Vorad [phoen] to analyse this, they in Neretva 93 want to mop up the Neretva River valley and come up to the borders of the HVO. Do you know about that and is that something that this document shows? Did you know about it? Were you aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it at the time, and just -- you mentioned right at the beginning when you started cross-examining me about whether I saw any signatories of any commander other than a Muslim, and I mentioned that I had met armija commanders who weren't Muslim. I couldn't remember the name, but I see it here. It is Stjepan Siber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is signed here Stjepan Siber, and he is the person that I was referring to. I believe that he is a -- of Serb origin, serving in the armija forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, within the frameworks of the document we've just been reading from, did you know that during the '93 offensive the BH army on the territory of Mostar brought in artillery support from the Serbs against the HVO in the offensive?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that but I am not surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Their Honours have already seen this document, so we'll move on. We still have some time, and I'd like to show a video on another subject and then we'll discuss it once we've seen the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Voiceover: "One month after the war started in 1992 --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Mostar. Voiceover: "The Mujahedin arrived in the land of Bosnia and formed two jihad camps. The first was in Central Bosnia. The second was situated in an area called Meholic [phoen], which is close to the city of Travnik. There was also a presence of Mujahedin brothers in Turbe and Radine [phoen], which lie between Travnik and Doniva [phoen]. These efforts were carried out under the leadership of Sef Habu Abdul Adiz [phoen], who was one of the first people to arrive in Bosnia from the Arabian peninsula. There he met the Mujahed Sef Anwar S'Aban [phoen], and together they agreed on the importance of initiating and carrying out jihad efforts in Bosnia to give victory to the Muslims and repel the enemy aggressors. "The second group kidnapped a vice commander of the Croat forces in Bosnia, along with six Croat soldiers. The news of the kidnap spread quickly and the disbelieving United Nations began to search for the kidnappers. They blockaded the roads and began to search everywhere. This meant that the brothers had to remain and hide in the forests despite the snow, the intensive cold, and the loss of communication with the command centre Mehovic. The plight of the Mujahedin prisoners did not concern the UN, fairly illustrating the hypocrisy. The UN accused the Mujahedin of being terrorists and war criminals. The command then came from the Bosnian army to release the Croatian prisoners but it was not obeyed. The next day, whilst the commander of the Croatian forces was driving to work in Zenica, the Mujahedin blocked off his route from in front and behind him with the objective of taking him and those with him as prisoners, but his personal bodyguard started firing at the Mujahedin. The Mujahedin sprayed the car with gunfire, killing everyone inside with the exception of one person. And here, Allah's will, we demonstrated in that the Croat commander remained alive and what was written by Allah happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Voiceover: "During this period the brothers gathered for a debate and discussed the recent events, and Wahiudeen, Allah have mercy upon him, handed over the leadership to Dr. Adul Harith [phoen] From Libya, due to him having the necessary qualifications and characteristics for this role. This gave Wahiudeen more time to concentrate on military affairs. Political associations and. Abdul N'Ali [phoen] took over leadership of the Mujahedin in Zenica. Dr. Abul Harith approached the Muslim forces and asked them to inform the world of the kidnap operation but they failed to do anything. Abul Harith then approached the UN forces present in Zenica. There was a great uproar and the disbelieving United Nations moved quickly now, attaching high priority to this issue. "Negotiations then took place concerning a prisoner exchange under the supervision of Wahiudeen, Nabu Nari [phoen] and the ranks of the Mujahedin. In the May of 1993, the prisoner exchange took place. It was a historical event which will never be forgotten, and the brothers being released from the Croatian prison and their feet touching the land of jihad once again, the brothers prostrated to Allah upon their release thanking Allah. "[No interpretation] Voiceover: "In Guca Gora, those brave enough to venture outside were preparing to bury their dead. Seven in all killed in yesterday's battle. There was no priest there, and so the army chaplain took charge of the funeral service. The gunmen in the surrounding hills tried to prevent these people from paying their last respects, but as British Army snipers took cover, the chaplain read on. "The attack continued until the army replied with 340 rounds from their chain guns. It was then that the commanding officer decided to evacuate the monastery, giving orders for the families to be transported inside the its armoured warriors. "[Indiscernible] Voiceover: "After capturing Guca Gora, the Mujahedin advanced to capture a fortified mountainous area under the leadership of Hasam Abdin [phoen], Allah have mercy upon him."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Voiceover: [Interpretation] "... by Bosnian Muslim soldiers during the conflict with Bosnian Croats. Those crimes has stayed virtually unknown to the general public overshadowed bit media and political cliche that Muslims were the only victims in the war against Bosnia-Herzegovina." "But one negative consequence of the war certainly has been the increasing radicalisation of the Muslim population and that's probably not a -- not a good sign because it does not -- does not help Bosnia integrate itself within Europe. "[No interpretation] "[No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "[No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know, witness, that this is the Muderiz Brigade in Jablanica, this crew here?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voiceover: [Interpretation] "The 4th Light Muslim Brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that unit also known as the Black Swans?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was known as Muderiz. A religious person, a cleric, led it. It's true they were in the same area as Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll need to have a break, Mr. Praljak. Do you have a question to put to the witness about the video footage we've just watched?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, here's my first question. I'll show you a document demonstrating how many Mujahedin they listed, but were you really aware -- after seeing this footage, were you truly aware of the strength of Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked in 1994 by the French Presidency of the ECMM to investigate the extent of Mujahedin activity. I wrote a special report, and I believe that report is available to this Court. And as I described yesterday, there were various units which one could attribute more extreme views right from those people that we -- some of those people we saw from externals who would, I think, fit anyone's description of Mujahedin, and we also saw elements there, I believe, of 17 Muslim Brigade, who were the indigenous. So I was certainly aware of the Mujahedin. In fact, I think I recognise one of those that I had an encounter with myself at Opera, and I was aware of the specific Muslim brigades that had a reputation for having a religious impetus to what they were doing and as something a little bit different from your mainstream armija, which you would have in most --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, please. Please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to be upsetting you, General Praljak. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, you're a soldier. Do you know the number of Mujahedin present then in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the number, but I do believe that I may have in that report made an estimate. I just can't pull it from my mind. So I don't know the number and can't give you a number at the moment, but there are documents in this court that -- where I think I have made an estimate. Certainly there were two specific Muslim brigades, so we are talking there in the region maybe of 500 in each brigade, so a thousand. Then we have some externals. I don't know how many externals, but I did make an estimate in that report. So it depends on your definition of Mujahedin, whether you mean those from outside of the country, indigenous. It is quite a difficult issue, and that's why we took some care in writing a report about it. But they were there, if that's the point. They were there, we knew they were there, and on those videos I saw them operating in those areas. I was at Guca Gora on that day. I was bearing those people. We were giving first aid to the survivors. I was in that church. So I was a witness to that. I went to Maline. I wasn't to the areas where the Mujahedin operated, where we had not previously had access. So I was aware of them. We tried to get as much information as we could about them, and I wrote various reports about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Let's talk about time. You've used more than 70 minutes. In other words, you have one hour and 10 minutes left, at the most. Second thing, when we are dealing with text in a document, a very long portion of text, rather than reading out the text, when you put the question to a witness just say, "In this document it is stated such-and-such things," summing up the text. Everybody has the text in front of them and they can check that the summary you're giving is accurate. Because if not, we're going to waste a lot of time reading out long portions of text because -- before putting your question. So just give us a summary of the text and then put your question to the witness. Yes, Mr. Kovacic, you wanted to comment on something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's not forget about this. I wanted an IC number for this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, there are four videos. Mr. Registrar, can we have numbers for the videos, IC numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the four videos that were shown by the Defence will be IC numbers 576 through IC 580 -- or 579. I stand corrected. IC 576 through IC 579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And that's in the order of the videos that were played to us, video one, two, three, and four. Mr. Praljak, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, on these pictures did you recognise any high-placed official of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the inspection of units crying "Allahu Akbar"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see in this video footage, at least three tanks of the BH army in Zenica, and later on two more?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw images of tanks. I forget the exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see that at Guca Gora members of the BH army desecrated the fresco above the altar in that church?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 3D 00920. It's a document that was already produced before this Court, but I would like Mr. Watkins to see it too. It's a reply by the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina sent to our Defence team, and it is a list of foreign nationals. Have you found it, Mr. Watkins?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a simple document. It's a list of foreign nationals, members of the 3rd Corps, and a list of foreign nationals in the Handzar Division. I wanted only two of these, although there are more. You can add up these two numbers, 1.774 and 717. That makes 2.491 foreign nationals, and it's signed by Major Hajrudin Grabovac, dated 15 July 1990 -- sorry, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, in order to check the veracity of this statement of yours, you're saying that all these people listed here are foreign nationals, but I see that number 224 is called Adilovic Besim, and that he is from Travnik. In other words, we don't have only foreign nationals on this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. I was mistaken, Your Honour. So the people listed are those who declared themselves as Mujahedin, and they include both local residents and foreign nationals. I probably added this up correctly anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just one question. Do you believe this list is complete, and do you think that in their training camps there were many more people who are not on this list?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reaction to this is that it's a much longer list than I would have expected. My own estimation of foreign nationals would be in the hundreds and not, as you've totaled, 1.774 plus, in fact over 2.000. I am surprised, but I have no way of verifying this is accurate or not. It's not what I saw on the ground in terms of numbers of foreign Mujahedin. The numbers in total, picking up the point which was made by Your Honour, I gave a number of brigades, the Muslim brigades, and mentioned that there were two that I was aware of with numbers round about 500. So if you were to add those to a thousand and then my estimation I think in what report is -- is a couple of hundred externals then, perhaps the figures get a bit closer. But as many externals as you are saying, this is a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, I want to say that there are books by foreign authors to dealt with the subject, and the number is usually between 4.500 and 5.000, but we'll deal with it later. Can we now just see P 02849. It's among the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just before we move on from the last exhibit. Perhaps I missed it. If I did, I apologise. What are the dates of this? What are the relevant dates in the last document as to the members of the alleged -- members of the alleged foreign nationals? I don't see any date on the document except 2005. The time period this relates to. Perhaps Mr. Praljak could assist the Chamber with providing the information for what time period this information is supposedly accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our request was to list foreign nationals in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it says clearly members of foreign nationals in the 3rd Corps, in the 4th Muslim Brigade, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as of what time, in 2005 or in 1993 or in 1999, or what time period does this information relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I wanted us to save time. As for document 3D 00920, we have two lists here. The first list refers to the 3rd Corps with 717 people, individuals, the majority of them being foreign nationals from Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Palestine, et cetera, and we have a second list with 1.774 individuals. It is entitled "El Mujahedin." I suppose that's the El Mujahedin unit. And for the dates now, we have a column here. One of them is "in" and the other one is "out." For example if we look at number 1, Mr. Aba Ktab, who is from Saudi Arabia, we see that he entered or saw he came in on the 22nd of July, 1995 and he left on the 22nd of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do I understand, then, that Your Honour is talking about second list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the second list. Mr. Aba is number 1 on the first list, the El Mujahedin list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question - my request remains, Your Honour, as to the date of the first list, which doesn't appear to be any dates indicated. All I'm asking is that it please be pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, as for the first list, do you have any dates or don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have dates. This is what I officially received. As far as the second document is concerned, the date is not when the person joined the unit but when he was put on record. It's only in 1995 they started to include these persons in their lists of troops, after the creation of the Federation. They started making a list, and the list of course is not complete, because by that time many people had left, but I'm facing time constraints here, and anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a very brief interruption.
