It seems that the first list is drawn up from the second list, because in the second list we find the name of Aba Ktab at number 1 and this person is found in the other list except with the difference that the date of birth is stated here, 1974. So the first list must have been drawn up from the second list, and in the first list we have 717 people drawn from the second list. But, Mr. Praljak, I gather that you do not have any additional information to give us about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Another observation must be made with regard to the second list. If you look, for instance, at page 3DT at the bottom, number 1736. You have Trsemovic [phoen] Osman, who is indicated with the dates 17 September 1993 to 18 September 1993. So he seems to have been there one day, and it is quite clear that this is not a list of the foreigners that at one particular moment in time were all together serving with the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I didn't claim otherwise. I just said this is a list I received through official channels, although the information in our possession says that by the time when this list was made most the foreign nationals had already left the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But now I would like us to move to P 02849. It's a report from your service, dated 19th June -- sorry, 5th June 1993. Do you have the document before you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have that document. Sorry, mine is dated the 19th of June. Sorry, yes, the 19th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, 19th of June, 1993. The report says, if you look at it, that television depicts obviously a different reality, that the report was made by an Englishman, a Swede, and a Greek, and it says, "Was it deliberate as many examples of collusion between Serbs and Croats before the events intend to demonstrate it or only the use of and opportunity at a time when Bosnian Croats want to reach their final goal, the recognition of Herceg-Bosna as a separate state?" And in the following paragraph we read: "Some people could wonder how Croats could accept to drive their own people to despair for political purposes." And it says: "... the Bosnian Croats are not going to be allowed to make completely disappear millions of Muslims whatever their wish and temptation to follow the example of the Serbs may be." Et cetera, et cetera. This report signed by Jean-Pierre Thebault, and you will probably see it on the third page of the English translation, it says: "Fact-finding has begun about devastation in Guca Gora village. One hundred eighty-one Croat civilians found shelter in the church. One civilian was found wounded." My question is -- I'm going to show you another document, since you are mentioned here. What were those Croatian acts that drove their own civilians to despair, or is it the case that the other side drove Croat civilians to despair and made them leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very interesting question, General Praljak, and I believe it's not such a simple answer. The feeling was, and I think Jean-Pierre Thebault, the French head of -- the French head of the regional centre, is noting something which is that it appeared that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was advantageous in terms of territorial allocation to the Bosnian Croats, and we noted earlier that they were quick to sign up to delivering the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and that would see certain cantons, and forgive me, I think it was canton 10 was based on -- on Travnik. It gave them a particular advantage in terms of running that municipality. The part of the Vance-Owen Plan, or at least part of the way it seemed to be interpreted on the ground was that there was a requirement by the majority army force in that canton, so in the case of canton 10 being allocated to the government by the Croats then, that the HV would be -- HVO, sorry, very clear clarification, HVO would be the military force there and that other soldiers would be required, i.e., armija soldiers would be required to lay down their weapons. Now, what we saw in Central Bosnia when the Vance-Owen Peace Plan collapsed seemed to be that there was a -- an attempt in Central Bosnia initially for the HVO to gain territory, but that was unsuccessful. Perhaps there was an overestimation of the HVO capability in Central Bosnia either to take territory or to enforce this compliance of armija handing over their weapons, and there was certainly never any intention from the armija that we came across that they were going to lay down their weapons or join the HVO forces. So what we then saw was, as so often happens when there are negotiations going on or even preceding or just after, military activity to seize territory, basically on the principle of who holds that territory has bargaining chips. So the attempt to establish the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, its organs of civilian and military infrastructure around Travnik, didn't happen, and the consequence there was that armija went on the offensive, and that then led to the things that you see me describing in the reports and that I've characterised earlier, which is in fact that the Bosnian Croat community, instead of being on the offensive and on the ascendance in central Travnik, it comes straight into the defensive position. They are defeated militarily in certain areas. Novi Travnik we've mentioned earlier, and later the fighting between Zenica through Maline, Guca Gora, down to Travnik, and we see those forces that were in the Travnik HVO units going into the pockets, and we get to a stage when there's a balance of forces again, and, as I described yesterday in this, what was largely infantry exchanges, we find concentrated pockets where the HVO, protecting the Bosnian Croat population, get to a stage when there is enough force within that pocket to resist any further attacks. Now, in that we saw some interesting things happening. In Travnik, when will the Muslims were successful -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to stick to documents and may we move on, because we've heard that yesterday. I do apologise. However -- well, you mentioned Maline. Now, in this same document there is the mention of Bando [phoen] Bukovica that you mentioned, Han Bila, Maline, and so on. Now I'd like you to take a look at 3D 00322, please. 322 are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd once again like to tell the Judges that this can't be considered quid pro quo, that this is information, facts about what happened on the ground, and the Prosecution case mentions this, whether the people actually fled from realistic danger and how the war evolved. But anyway, the document I'd like to focus on now is 3D 00322.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you what you know about it. Look at Konjic, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not found the document yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D 00322. It's a separate document. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have a separate document, but that is 374.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate you're asking me to look at 322, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's the first -- third from the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Look at Mostar, please. You can see Grabovica on the 9th of September, 1993. Thirty-two victims in Grabovica. Did you know about that crime, or whatever you'd like to call it, on the 9th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it. This is the one we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn to Jablanica municipality, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a document -- sorry, a page number that you can help me get there quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Jablanica. It's the next page. It says Jablanica. So look at Jablanica, Doljani. That will speed matters up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it would be easier if you would just give us the last three numbers of the page so that will enable us to go directly to the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it goes in order: Mostar, Jablanica, then it says Doljani. Now, as to page numbers 3D 13178. 178 are the digits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 173, Doljani, the 28th of July, 1993, 63 victims, 63 casualties. Did you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Praljak, I'm being very slow this morning. You just need to pause for one second while I find that page and then I'll be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document and the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is this: During that time or immediately after it did you know anything about this occurrence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Doljani.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we now look at the next part, which is Konjic, and the page number is 180. On that page we have Gostovici, Gorani, Trusina, Radesine, and those places and others. Did you know about any of those places as being the localities where 85 individuals of Croatian nationality were massacred? And you can look at the following pages as well.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was aware of allegations of Trusina, Zabrdje, and those are the only ones I recognise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn to page 185, which is Prozor. Uzdol and Hudotsko?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I was aware of Uzdol and referred to it earlier in giving witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 14th of September, 1993, in Uzdol, 41 fatalities, and that's on page 186 you'll find that figure, during the operation of Neretva 93. And on page 187, Udolsko [as interpreted] two days later, 24 fatalities. Did you know about Hudotsko?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Hudotsko, but I know the village well, Uzdol. It was central to earlier discussions at the beginning about January February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now open the page to 1793, which is Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look at the names there, Bugojno, Kula, Gravica, Vuci Polje [phoen], et cetera. Did you know that in those localities 118 persons were killed, and do you know any of the names of places mentioned here. And you can look at the next page, too.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Vrbanja and obviously Bugojno itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I can inquire. Just so the record is clear and to assist the witness, the Chamber knows by this point in the trial that a number of towns and villages have different names. They may have a Muslim name. They may have a Croat name, and perhaps Mr. Praljak can assist us in any -- if any of these villages or places have another name by which the witness may know them. Because when he says he doesn't recognise a name, maybe it's a completely different name than the one he knows. So it's not completely fair to suggest that he doesn't know these locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if you know the equivalent name of a village, if you know two different names of a village, you may do so. You may tell the witness what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just two names are different in Croatian and according to the Bosnia. Prozor and Rama and Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf. Those are the equivalents. All the other place names are the same for Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, Mr. Watkins, would you look at 197 now, please, which was Travnik municipality. You were there at the time and take a look at the place names. You'll see Maline mentioned. You'll see Dolac Bila. And then the following pages the number of fatalities, and tell us what you knew about this and what you reported on, and you can glance at the dates too.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the names Mehurici, Travnik obviously, Orasac, Guca Gora, Maline, Novi Travnik going further on, yeah. So that's it. Oh, Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Very you knew that crimes had been committed there.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew there were allegations, and I then investigated and wrote reports about them. Maline is a good example of where we've tried very hard to establish what had happened there, but we did not come across the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now we're going to skip over some things and go to page 233, which is Kakanj municipality, which in June 1993, after an attack by the BH army, led to the population leaving the municipality, and all this turned out to be under the organisation of the political leadership of the Croatian Defence Council. So take a look at what happened at that time in Kakanj municipality. Take a look at -- on the 18th of May, nine fatalities; three fatalities in Trubici on the 13th of June; Lijeska, Balici, seven fatalities there; Kraljeva Sutjeska, 13th to the 23rd of June, six victims; Zlatnice, five on the 30th of June. Can you see all that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, as you've seen all this information, tell me, please, what was it that made the Croats -- or let me ask you this: Do you know how many soldiers of the 3rd Corps the BH army had?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers the 2nd BH army corps had?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers there were under the command of Tihomir Blaskic in Central Bosnia, including Zepce, Kakanj, et cetera? What was the total number of men he had under him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know of a single order which would be characterised as offensive to his army, which we saw later numbered some 10.000 soldiers to attack nine to ten times stronger army that had surrounded him? Would this professional soldier as you called him engage in such madness? Do you know of any offensive axis of attack in Central Bosnia towards the Muslims except in defence, for defensive purposes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any order. We saw tactical attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, correct, tactical attacks. Now, while you were in Mostar and up there, do you know whether I issued any order which was an offensive order against the BH army, except for one which was Rastani when we wanted to gain control there? A single HVO offensive against the BH army, or was it only defence from the Neretva offensive 93?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any specific orders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, is it true and correct and it says in your reports that after the fall of Bugojno, as we interpret it, there was a continuous attack by the BH army launched against Gornji Vakuf towards Prozor which lasted between five and six weeks?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I spoke to the armija commanders, and I believe at that time, sir, that I met you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, can you tell me during that period of time, and all these operations, action from Bugojno towards Gornji Vakuf and the offensives, how many times the road that you called Diamond stopping the passage of international humanitarian aid or when it says in your reports Diamond was opened or when there were strong fighting around Makljen, when that route was closed to humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something of a lottery when one travelled from Central Bosnia to Herzegovina. It was regularly closed but not always by one -- not always by the Croat forces; sometimes by the armija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer, but my question was very precise, and we can read that in your reports that Diamond was opened. From the south side, the Croatian side, apart from when there was intensive fighting near the road at Makljen, when was that road closed, and did the convoys going into Central Bosnia, were they able to move unobstructed from us? Tell me when that was.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were regular obstructions coming up into Central Bosnia of convoys. I have to look at the documents or you -- someone would have to produce them, but you'll see where we stated that they are closed. There was no way that one travelled from Herzegovina up into Central Bosnia and anticipated clear routes and unobstructed. You were often stopped. I spent quite a few hours at Makljen ridge myself. I think most of the time it may have been local issues, but never mind, we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not challenging that, that there were local issues, but each and every convoy with its problems, were the problems solved so that the convoys could actually reach their destination ultimately? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes with delays. There were some significant things. Not at the Makljen ridge but like the movement of the hospital, which I don't think was resolved, or at least not for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now P 05356 is the next document I'd like us to look at, please. 5356. It is a daily report for the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: A daily summary, as I said. P 05356 is the document number. It is a document by your service, and the date is the 24th of September, 1993. It was signed by Mr. Martin Garrod and relates to talks --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this document. One moment, please. I'm looking in the Prosecutor's file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's in the other one, Witness. It's in the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the document. The Prosecution took me to the Prosecution file. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, it says here under point 2, Political Activity, "M9." Who was M9?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, 24 of September, that would have been -- that would have been either Jesus Amatriain or Martin Garrod. I can't remember exactly when Jesus Amatriain took over from Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. It says that there was a meeting with me.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I can clarify that. If we go to the end of the document you will see that it is Martin Garrod who is HCC Mostar. And HCC, their call-sign was Mike 9. So this is Martin Garrod meeting me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your document it says that I said over there that I would turn off the water supply if winter sets -- when winter sets in, and that I would not allow humanitarian aid to go through. I don't know who translated for you, but my question is this, and we saw the maps yesterday: Had I wanted to cut off the water supply, had I been that type of warrior, tell me what place could you cut off the water supply to the opposite side? Where? What place would that have been where you could have shut off the water supply?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I first begin by saying this is not my report, but in my earlier testimony it I did state that you said that. Well, you have a certain characteristic style of engagement, and in that engagement you told me that you disliked intensely, in fact I believe the word translated as "hated" the armija. You wanted to defeat the armija, and you would do so by whatever means you had, stop water, stop humanitarian aid. It was just what was translated to me. You could stop humanitarian aid. I would need to look a little bit at where water sources were, and supplies too, to be able to answer this, your specific question about water.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that was what was translated for you. I don't know what was translated, but what I'm asking you is this, because I don't think I can be considered an entirely stupid man: Tell me, where could you shut off the water even if I had wanted to, or do you think it's a nonsensical sentence, because there is no possibility of doing that there because Kruscica was under BH army control, so there wasn't a single locality where the HVO could shut off the water supply had it even wanted to do so. But let's move on. If you can't remember a place where the water supply could have been cut off, if you can't name a place name, then never mind. I remember I spoke about fuel, but we'll come to that in due course. Can you name a single place where the HVO could cut off the water supply, shut down the water?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I said I would need to look at -- I can't remember off the top of my head, but there were some interesting underground connections around the lakes around Prozor and down towards Jablanica. I'm not quite sure where the water was flowing, but that's what I -- in terms of Kruscica, you're absolutely correct in that particular case. In Central Bosnia we were regularly dealing with issues of water being cut off, and in that case it was the Muslim community cutting off the water to Vitez, but also, of course, it effected their own population in Zenica. That's all I can give in regards to water supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient for me. Now, I speak at length here about the fact that Croatia offered Ploce, which were built for -- well, I won't go into that section. All I want to ask you is this, and that's something that you refer to as well, and that is the question of the helicopter which took a girl from Rumbok, who suffered from leukaemia, and her parents to Split. And in this document it is to be found -- let me just take a moment to find it. I can't find it. But do you remember that an HVO helicopter took a girl and her parents from Rumbok near Prozor or Rama to Split during the time that you talked to me? So that was a Muslim family and their child.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's in the report somewhere, because I've read it. Look at this conversation about the BBC, page 2, 2 of 4, where it says that at one point I demanded that the BBC go first to Konjic and Bugojno. I spoke about Dretelj as a bad thing, and then it goes on with and commentary that "Praljak, after that, let the BBC go, but he only wanted to emphasise the need to establish who was responsible for those crimes." It's on page 4 of 4. "Praljak obviously gave in when BBC addressed him personally as suggested by the chief of UNHCR. BBC has the freedom to and plans to stay." Just the last sentence. "Bearing in mind his emphatic statements, it's interesting why General Praljak changed his mind about BBC's entry into Mostar. The most likely explanation is that he had the opportunity to emphatically state his views to the BBC crew as to what they were doing wrong, in his opinion, and he used that opportunity. Having done that, he was prepared to give them permission to enter. That would have been in character for him from what we were able to see at the meeting." Do you know that the BBC did indeed receive permission to film what they wanted, and do you believe it is indeed in character for me to state my views strongly but that my conduct was perfectly normal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the BBC. I do believe that you state your position strongly, and I do remember in my own reports of meeting with you that I asked for access to the imam of Prozor, for instance, and that that did happen afterwards. Not consistently from that point ever on, but certainly I did get access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me find another document. P 04431. P 04431.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Praljak, will I find that in your file?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, Mr. Watkins. That's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I would just like to refer to paragraph 1 of this document of the 20th of August, where it says a hunger strike was going on at the hospital in Toplice, that the strike has begun to draw attention to the suffering of Croats wounded in Central Bosnia, and so on. Were you aware that, due to the reporting, such as it was it, seriously wounded persons in hospitals in Toplice and elsewhere went on a hunger strike in order to force somebody, at least, to start reporting in a more unbiased and truthful way what was going on in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this links in with this whole discussion about trying to make sure that the Bosnian Croat voice was heard more effectively, and in this case it seems to be that those who are obviously distressed are going on strike and that will gain immediate attention, and it is part an attempt to get your perspective across. The reference to the hospitals in Travnik and Vitez, I was directly involved in organising the evacuation of the first evacuation of Nova Bila by convoy down through Herzegovina. Unfortunately, I was unsuccessful at the same time to evacuate the hospital from Travnik to Zenica. I was prevented to do -- from doing so by HVO forces, who I believe were reporting directly to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Look at P 04363.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Political activity. That's number 2. "Beba the security officer of the BH army said that the army would never allow for a helicopter evacuation of Bila because HVO helicopters were frequently seen unloading ammunition." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at the next page, 2 of 2. "Civilian police in Bugojno identified 145 Muslims and Croats that were killed in -- during the fighting." It doesn't say how many were Croats, how many Muslims, and whether all of them were fighting men. Do you see that? It's the first line on page 2.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Viktor 2 finally gained access to the Muslim population and prisoners in Prozor. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says they discovered -- it's about Bugojno. They discovered -- I don't know if we are looking at the same document. P 04363 of the 20th August 1993.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at that document, Mr. Praljak, and when I turn to the second page of that document, the first --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: About Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that, interestingly. I have Viktor 2 finally gained access to the Muslim population. It appears that it's on the first page in the copy I have. Yes, I've now found what you're referring to. "Civilian police in Bugojno have identified 145 bodies, Croat Muslim, killed in the fighting."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It does not say how they were killed. The report does not specify it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But it mentions 167 prisoners in an engineering school, Croats, of course; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that we're now talking about Viktor 2 finally gained access to the Muslim population and prisoners in Prozor. They revealed 167 prisoners being held at the tech school. So that's Prozor. You're holding them, Mr. Praljak, but you have given us access to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. In passing, one -- in one report you say that after the crime in Uzdol, the one -- and the one two days later, there was no retribution and the situation in Prozor remained quiet. Do you recollect that after those two crimes you got access to the imam and there was no retribution whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember writing a report about there being no retribution. I cannot definitively say in the same report that that's when we got access to the imam, but, as I say, you did give us access to the imam.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document under item 8, "3rd Corps of the army obstruction many initiatives, be they from the HVO or international organisations in cases of exchanges of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak needs to read more slowly. We did not get that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All this has to do with the helicopters for which we have no time. Is it correct that there were major obstructions created by the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had regular issues with regards to freedom of movement and access issues. And the comment here is that, "it's on the increase and probably on the back of hardening attitude that developed following their military successes in the Vrbas Valley and the Lasva valley," or least the north end of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could we now see document P 04363.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we go to the document could I request a short break? I just need to go to the loo. It is well known I have a very small bladder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 12.00. We will have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. You have 25 more minutes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, P 05162. It's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a report by your organisation, dated 17 September 1993. Under General Situation it says: "Situation relatively quiet in Central Bosnia except in Gornji Vakuf, which has seen fierce fighting in early morning. Diamond route continues to be open."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we then agree that fighting in Vakuf and towards Prozor continues to go on and the route is still open? Is your report correct on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report written by one of my teams and sent to me, and on that day it is open, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And how would you comment this: "... continues to be open"? That implies that it was open before. This is not the only document speaking of this. Regardless of difficulties that I do not deny, but it does say,; "Continues to be open."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my translation -- or in the original, rather, it is "Route Diamond remains open." It is interesting that the bothered to put this in. If there was no problem then they wouldn't have put it in at all. I also note under the Political Situation a reference to trying to gain access to the imam of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that you did get access to the imam in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. The specific comment says, "Croat authorities in Prozor making it difficult for V2 to visit the imam of Prozor and is being isolated from the community," and one of the things we're looking to build confidence is it appears that the team is trying to involve the Roman Catholic priest. So we are saying there was difficulty on that day, but I am also clearly stating, and have earlier, that we did get -- after me asking you, we did get access to the imam.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. It says up here, Political Situation, "the population in Prozor calmly accepted the massacre in Uzdol and so far there have been no cases of mistreatment of the Muslim community. Tensions are growing and Muslims feel there is a growing danger of violence against them." You noted those two massacres over two days resulting in over 60 people killed. You have a lot of experience, after all, in these matters. Do you think it was simple to prevent and stop retribution over those incidents in two villages that have a total population taken together of 600 in a war like that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been easy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does it seem logical to you that a person in that situation placed the imam in isolation and under protection waiting for a couple of days until hundreds of talks are conducted, and until all that has been reduced to a tolerable measure after a crime like that? Does that sound reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- I'm not perhaps understanding the question directly, but basically I think what you're asking is is it unreasonable in those circumstances we found it difficult to get to the imam. I would accept that, but I would also suggest that it would -- we would also, and you would have also have known, that the Muslim community would have been very, very fearful and that an international community visiting them at that moment would have been of some succor to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I agree, sir, but tell me: There was fighting in Gornji Vakuf. The other side was attacking. Did you get access to the imam? Did imam after that visit some Muslim families? Is all that correct? Did I, when I arrived, of course, back from the field, give you access to the imam?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That question is answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. Do you believe it was unreasonable for me to place guards around the imam in a situation like that, and does it seem logical to you that hundreds of meetings had to be held to prevent retribution after these two massacres? Let me address you in person and in the first person singular.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not believe it was unreasonable to place guards, but having that protection there would also have been no reason why we shouldn't have visited as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you did visit him after I came back from those meetings, but never mind. Let us look at number 4, Humanitarian Activity. It says: "Team V2 visited the child suffering from leukaemia that the HVO transported to Split. Mother and child are well and found accommodation in town. The HVO brought the family to the hospital and left them there without extending any assistance as had been agreed earlier." So can we note that somebody from the HVO ordered a helicopter to fly, in the situation as it was, to bring that mother and child to Split? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no reference to a helicopter, and I see no reference to the ethnicity of the -- of the family. I merely see that the HVO facilitated the family move. It might have been a Bosnian Croat. I don't know. It must have been a Muslim. I don't know. It may have been by air. It may have been by road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In one report that I cannot locate at this moment has to do with Mr. Martin Garrod. It says clearly helicopter and the nationality is indicated. The intention was to go to Zurich. Do you know that somebody of Croat nationality was intending to go to Zurich after that rather than stay in Zagreb in the hospital? The objection here is that -- or seems to be that we brought that little girl and left her without extending any further assistance. What assistance can be expected, could be expected after bringing that child to the Split hospital?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't read any criticism. I'm just reading an explanation of a movement of a child suffering from leukaemia by the HVO. I don't see it as being criticised in any way, but neither, as I say, do I see any indication of the mode of transport or the ethnicity. The other report to which you refer of Martin Garrod's, I'm not aware of that report. It does not ring any bells for me, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. I will owe it to the Court to demonstrate that it was indeed a helicopter. Look at number 5. Violence against the Muslim minority that we expected at the outset has not occurred yet. So you, too, expected that after something like that a retribution might occur and slip out of control, because both the troops and the people who were killed were closely related by family ties.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the record, I believe you mean paragraph 8, Assessment. "The initial expected violence against the Muslim minority in Prozor has not yet happened." Yeah, we anticipated after the massacre of Croats at Uzdol there may be some reaction in Prozor, and here we're stating it hasn't happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did any retribution occur later, according to the information you had?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had, and it was referred to earlier in the evidence that I've given, of a large-scale movement of population from Prozor down to Jablanica, and I made some comment about whether this was -- how this was organised, whether the Muslim authorities in Jablanica were ready to accept them. I forget the exact dates, but I do believe it probably is after these dates.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. We'll see from documents later that this occurred before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, would you please put this on the ELMO before the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mentioned having clearly seen some unit of the Croatian army or, rather, a truck with writing on it indicating Osijek. Witness, how many trucks or buses have you in fact seen or did you see at that moment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I listed them or gave some indication in that report. I can't remember off the top of my head. I do remember listing some vehicle-mounted multi-barrel rocket launchers, some towed artillery, some coaches, I think, with -- yes, coaches with soldiers on and one or two other bits. Overall, my estimation, without going back to that report, we probably saw where between, I don't know, 25, 35 vehicles. A large number, a unit. A regiment perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many small vehicles and how many large vehicles were there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it be useful for us to go back to that document where I do list certain elements of equipment? I've given you my rough estimation. We're talking about a mixture of vehicles. We are talking about vehicles that are towing equipment. That would be heavy goods vehicle, lorry-type equipment, some moving without towing any equipment, the specific artillery I've mentioned, and transport with -- for people, i.e., coaches.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Look at this paper in front of you where I wrote, "a standard for a motorised brigade," and you see that the motorised brigade consisted of three motorised battalions, one armoured battalion, two artillery battalions for support, one anti-air defence battalion, one engineering battalion, one support battalion. That is the standard, approximately. The strength you have such a unit would be 4.600 to 5.000. The number of vehicles it has ranges from 6 to 800. And when these vehicles move in a convoy, which is intolerable, by the way, such a unit has 10 to 12 echelons with 50 to 70 lorries -- sorry, and it's 50 to 70 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have had the pleasure in my army service of leading such a convoy, but what you're describing here is a brigade move, and a brigade consists of, as you say, three battalions. I mentioned a -- a unit and called it a regiment. For those that are not of military background, certainly in the British forces a regiment would equate with a battalion, and what I'm saying is I saw about a regiment, a battalion. So one-third of all that you're describing at maximum. So I didn't see a whole brigade move. I saw a unit move, which I've estimated to be - maximum size - a regiment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at an armoured brigade, 3.200 to 3.500 soldiers. The total number of vehicles is 400 to 500. The length of convoy movement is 40 to 50 kilometres. Just tell me whether this is correct from all you know.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly speaking that would be an order of battle for the movement of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Because of time constraints I cannot call all the documents I wanted, but from that document we will later derive -- first of all, we don't know what it was up there and who was moving, but from what I read it was not a battalion. It was a company. So what you could have seen was a company, 170 to 200 soldiers; is that correct? Much closer to a company than to a regiment.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I would estimate it was more than a company size which I saw. I do mention a brigade number of 5 brigade, but, of course, that doesn't mean that the whole brigade is moving. Brigades, as you know, general, don't have to move in one unit, and what I saw here was less than a brigade, considerably less than a brigade, possibly a regiment, certainly more than a company. And for those that are not of military background, there are usually three fighting companies to a regiment plus a support company. So about four companies per regiment. Would you agree, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct, militarily speaking, but we shall come back to the exact estimate of the vehicles enumerated there and see if that's correct. Do you know how many tanks were captured by the HVO in liberating the barracks at Capljina, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many tanks and artillery we captured in liberating Mostar? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many howitzers, 152-millimetres, were in Travnik in Bratstvo at the beginning of the war that was split half-half with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know in the same factory how many multiple-rocket launchers there were that we last split half/half with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many coastal B-1 cannons there were in the same factory that we gave to Croatia and got in exchange something that was again split half/half with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many tanks and artillery pieces Colonel Siljeg had in his operative zone? Before you saw the column, that is.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I did see on one occasion a T-54, 55 in Prozor. So I only ever saw one -- or a couple of tanks in that area. One that I can distinctly remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the next document, 3D 00954, please. 3D 00954 is the number of the document. Did you --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what -- I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My first question is this: Did the BH army, while you were up there, have cars? We saw they had tanks, helicopters, small vehicles. They moved around in vehicles. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including my ECMM vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, does Bosnia-Herzegovina have petroleum sources? Oil fields.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Bosnia-Herzegovina but, yes, up in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, here we have documents from the Ploce port, the port of Ploce in Croatia. Take a look at them, please, and you'll be able to see the dates of the dozens of documents that I have. I've just prepared a few by way of information. You'll see the oil refinery mentioned, and you'll see the letters of import/export operations, bills of lading, the 14th of August, 1993, the 15th of August, 1993, you see fuel, diesel fuel. All that is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that uninterruptedly throughout the war the BH army had fuel supplies coming in for helicopters, tanks, vehicles generally, and other types of fuel, and did you wonder where they were getting this from? Did you know that it went via Croatia and via the HVO check-points in those convoys that moved around? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- it was of interest, and I was aware of various routes in, including through Serb territory and deals done with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, excuse me. I find this a bit difficult. You refer in a very general way to a bunch of documents which cover various merchandise. I looked at one of them. It is it the page 3D 25-0589, enterprise port Ploce Kardeljevo, I think. And I find no reference here, but I may not be alert enough. I do not find any reference here to -- to Bosnia or to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or anything else that would link the document to the case before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, as far as the port of Ploce is concerned you have metre long documents on every detail, but I just want to ask a specific question to it a professional soldier, which Mr. Watkins is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. I don't have metre-long documents. I have one here that you have presented the witness, and that's the one I'm talking about. We cannot talk about metres of documents that we do not have here. But I think Mr. Kovacic would like to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. I hope I can be of assistance. Since we have no reports showing one document which shows that merchandise X arrived on such-and-such a ship and continued along its route to the person it was being taken to, this set of documents that have been attached here as a good exam you always have to tie yourself to up a one good document. You have a document that applies to the port of Ploce, then the hauling country [as interpreted], et cetera. So you always have some link. You can either see the date, number, or the number of the document. Of course, from each individual document you won't be able to get the necessary information, but if you look at them as a set, as linked documents, then you will see exactly how the merchandise came in, what ship brought it in, what route the merchandise took, and so on and so on. But you're right. You can't see it from one document. That's why we put them into these packages or sets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you -- are you then suggesting, Mr. Kovacic, that it is for the Chamber to sort of link these together like a puzzle? I've often heard this is your case, so I would expect documents to be presented in a way that the Chamber sees the link, and so far these documents do not permit me to see it. I'm not saying it doesn't exist, understand me well, not at you will. But I cannot see it in this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, take a look at document on the incoming and outgoing fuel of 4.773.132 kilogrammes, D2. It arrived from the USSR to BiH, and the importer was Energopetrol.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir, is this: The company Energopetrol, was it a firm in Sarajevo under the control of the authorities of the -- or political authorities of the Muslims, of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Energopetrol, a Sarajevo-based company, as it says in the document, who is taking over the goods, who is importing the goods, and the importer in this case is Energopetrol. It was brought in by the ship called Columbia Erre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's what it clearly says there, Judge Trechsel. The only state company in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Energopetrol.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know about that, Mr. Watkins?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know -- I do know about Energopetrol. Indeed I -- when I set up that company after the war I tried to trade with Energopetrol and also with HINA. But how can I help further with this? If you were saying there was normal, regular economic transactions during the period of conflict, I would find that difficult to support and substantiate. If you're saying that deals and money was passed, and people made a lot of money out of moving goods outside of any legitimate customs and trading system, then I would certainly agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, sir. This followed the regular customs routes with all the control and paperwork attending it. There are no shortcomings. There's the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Muslim importer. You have the name of the supplier. You have the port of Ploce. You have the beneficiary, and all this is passing through Herceg-Bosna in the throes of the war. Now, do you agree with me it was merchandise that was not humanitarian aid but was used to put into motion the war machine of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at that time was engaged in the Neretva 93 offensive. Then we had the offensive on Gornji Vakuf, Makljen, and so on towards the western frontiers. So can you tell me where that example exists anywhere in the history of warfare that you were taught at school? So those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll pick -- there are several bits in there but let me say that it would have been very strange indeed when the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims were fighting to have allowed this regular traffic to be taking place. So one has to look at under what circumstances. I do not know. I see no reference in here, but this could well have been one of the fuel supplies that was brokered by UNHCR and would be part of a wider deal about distribution of humanitarian aid, because certainly fuel was taken under the auspices of the UN into Bosnia, and that would have arrived in Ploce and it ultimately would have been going into armija forces. So that's the only time I could -- could accept and understand that there was a regular ship arriving, unloading, taking its produce through -- sorry, it's cargo through, if there was some international supervision. Otherwise there would have been a lot of money exchanging hands. It is constant support -- surprise, indeed was to me, just the amount of trading that was done between those people who were fighting. It was extraordinary that somebody would be on a front line and be fighting each other, and yet trade was happening in order to pass ammunition to the troops on the front line to do that fighting. Extraordinary, but I witnessed it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up, Mr. Praljak. We are going to move on to the Judge's question before the redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You are in fact interpreting it this way. The cisterns, water tanks were passing throughout the war. Do you know that in Zagreb, with the recognition of the Croatian state and the defence ministry that there were places where UNHCR canned goods were opened, ammunition put in, and with our knowledge carried throughout had the war to the BH army? Do you know about that or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On earlier testimony I've said I believe there were substantiated cases sometimes where UNHCR vehicles had been found carrying something. But there were also just legitimate movements of petroleum as organised by UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, based on the comment you made a moment ago, I wasn't sure if the Judges were going to ask questions first or if the Prosecution was. Either way, I will have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have one question to put to the witness. It shouldn't take too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that you went to Mostar. You saw what was going on there. At various points you dealt with shelling, fire being opened, et cetera. You mentioned that. We've heard many witnesses talk to us about shelling and exchange of fire. At this stage it seems that some units were stationed around Mostar. These were HVO units, Muslim units from the ABiH, and there were also Serb units. At the time when you were in theatre, did you hear of or did you yourself see that sometimes the Serbs would open fire on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't other that in the time that I was there. But I do not discount the fact that could have happen. I just didn't observe it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. That was the only question I wanted to put to you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Watkins.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a few more questions before I hope we will be able to -- to let you go on about your business and life. You were asked a couple of questions or a number of questions for a time about some military decrees and who in the HVO chain of command, for example, you may remember there were questions about who could relieve a brigade commander, who could -- and could you tell the Judges, if you know, concerning Colonel Blaskic, at the time you knew him, he was the commander of something that in the HVO structure was called an operational zone or operative zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Operational zone middle Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know either by name of position, that is by structure, the box or the line on the chart, if you will, or by name, if you know, who during that time, during -- I think the questions were being particularly put to you around the time of Stupni Do in October of 1993, who Colonel Blaskic's superior was? And again either by function or if you know who held at that position at the time, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at that time it was General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Supreme Commander of HVO. You could argue that his first communications would have been with the staff at Citluk --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where the Chief of Staff may be -- or would be present, or should be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You had a number -- if I understand you correctly, you had various dealings with Colonel Blaskic during this time. Did Colonel Blaskic -- when I say "during this time," it's -- let's talk about perhaps the second half of 1993. Did he indicate to you who he considered to be his commanding officer, the person who he was reporting to and taking orders from at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only person that I ever heard Colonel Blaskic refer to as commander was General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I could ask the witness --.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with a couple of questions I'd like to put to the witness, if the witness could please be shown the Prosecution book of maps, which is Exhibit P 9276. I believe it's in e-court as well. I can't assist with much more than that except that it should be under -- in e-court as the same exhibit, P 97 -- excuse me, P 09276.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't believe you'll have it, sir. They should provide it to you, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, please. Before letting you go on, I have some doubt now in my mind following the answers I've heard given by the witness. The Prosecutor asked you whether Colonel Blaskic was the one in charge of the operational zone. You said yes. Then the Prosecutor asked you who was above him, and your answer is General Praljak. Then the Prosecutor at line 6, page 78, asked you who Colonel Blaskic was reporting to, and here your answer is General Petkovic. I do not understand. I'm confused. Is it General Praljak or General Petkovic. If in the operational zone Colonel Blaskic is in command, who is above him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the only time I ever heard Colonel Blaskic himself refer to a senior commander was General Petkovic. Depending on the time that we're talking about, it would either be General Petkovic, but when General Petkovic hands over to General Praljak, then Colonel Blaskic's ultimate commander would be General Praljak. The intermediary that I introduced to the Citluk headquarters is that there would be a chief of staff there. During the period when Colonel Blaskic was reporting to General Petkovic, I am unsure as to who was the Chief of Staff of the HVO. When Colonel Blaskic would have been reporting to General Praljak, my understanding is that General Petkovic at that time was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's still not very clear to me, but let's proceed. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you have the book of maps there. You've made an interesting point a couple of times and I would like to come back to. It's perhaps -- it's perhaps appropriate that we look at a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the first map in the book of maps that you have there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I say particularly appropriate, because I believe, if I'm not mistaken, today is the 15th anniversary of the admission of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a member state of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that regard, sir, if you have that map?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at that map, could you tell it us is that the map -- are those the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina that -- the international recognised borders that existed prior to the war, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are those the internationally recognised borders that also existed, if you will, after the war?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, can you assist us in this: Prior to the time, for example, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna declared its existence in November 1991, did Bosnia have access to the sea?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a -- there's -- part of the physical border is at the sea; that is Neum. In terms of trading it would have gone out of its border and into Croatia and primarily through Ploce, but, yes, there is an international boundary that is to the Adriatic at Neum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that at the time of the -- prior to the war and prior to the conflict with the HVO that Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory of the internationally recognised entity Bosnia-Herzegovina, included not just part of Mostar but all of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And likewise, and my final question on this point, just taking the example of Central Bosnia, all of Central Bosnia was possessed by and part of the internationally recognised territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in terms of the Muslims wanting access to the sea and the HVO granting them access to the sea, that's something they already had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you to -- you were asked questions and if I understood some of the cross-examination, the suggestions at least in some instances seemed to be that either your reporting, your personal reporting, or the reporting of the ECM was somehow biased against the Croats or in -- or in favour of the Muslims or that certain things that happened to the Croats were not adequately reported or reported at all, for that matter. I would like to give you an opportunity to further address that, and my question to you, Mr. Watkins, is: Do you consider that during your tours of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, your tenure there, did you attempt to report developments, facts on the ground on all sides as they related to all sides to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question. The gentleman's integrity has never been in question. No one has intimated that this gentleman was in any way, shape, or form was subjective to one side or the other. While there may have been insinuations that members within the ECMM or within other international agencies were biased one way or another, under no circumstances, and I want the record to be clear that -- that the Defence has challenged the integrity of this particular witness. In other words, I have gone out of my way to praise this witness as being one of the very few that we've seen, perhaps the only one that we've seen thus far, who'd been objective, and his reporting speaks of that. What we have challenged is that he has operated with less than all the information, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- with all respect to my good friend, Mr. Karnavas, he may have -- that may be his position. That is not the suggestions and the attacks that I heard on the witness through all of the cross-examination. And in fact, even what Mr. Karnavas has just said apparently is that even other ECMM witnesses apparently have been less than -- had been less than candid with the Court. So while we have Mr. Watkins here, I'd like him to tell us his view to the best of his knowledge about the balanced nature of ECMM's reporting in general, to the best of their ability, and to your own, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's where I -- now there's a different twist. If he wants to ask the gentleman about his balanced approach, of course he can comment. As far as the ECMM I don't see how he can comment on other individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He had number of other people under his command who made reports on a regular basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping] If I may, Your Honour, if I may. First of all this was developed on cross-examination how they would go about gathering information, so it's not necessary. It's before the Trial Chamber. So it's really in the appropriate redirect examination. So I think we've counted it. We've heard other witnesses. Other witnesses have been challenged for their bias in reporting. This gentleman has not. If he wishes him now to ask again to reopen his direct examination as to what his approach was, that's fine, but I think it's irrelevant. The documents presented to the gentleman that he generated speak for themselves, and I for one have never challenged the gentleman's reporting system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Without going into a debate about the absence or not of bias, the interesting question that we could put to you is the following, Witness: When an ECMM member drafted a report, would he or she draft that report as independently as possible, as impartially as possible, without taking into account the involvement of X or Y? You yourself have drafted a number of reports. You know your colleagues. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aim was, sir, that each monitor should report impartially, and I believe that the product of our work was our reports, and getting accurate and fair assessment was our main aim. It was clear sometimes that monitors that spent a long time in one particular area, be that within the armija area or within HVO area, they would sometimes begin to accept at face value what was presented to them, and to use an English phrase, perhaps go native. And so I was always very careful to rotate monitors, and if I detected anything that looked bias then would take the appropriate action. But I do believe that the quality of the ECMM reports, certainly it's varied, but overall it was -- it was impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was going to take the witness through several other of his reports -- other of his reports as examples but given the answer he's just given I won't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I would like to ask you this as my final question or two. If I could ask you to look, if you still have the Prosecution bundle, at Exhibit P 02849, which is early in the binder 2849. Mr. Praljak at one point, among others, perhaps, was asking you about.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm told they're in both bundles but as long as you have one or the other. 2849. This is the report dated the 19th of June, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can ask you to look please at that fourth paragraph on the first page and that says, and this is the same one Mr. Praljak referred you to: "Some people could wonder how Croats could accept to," and I'm just reading from the page, "to desperate their own people for political purposes." Now, you began to give a full answer to that question and about -- and if you want to look on to orient yourself to the rest of that paragraph and on over to the next page, and let me just stop for a moment and ask you -- if you turn over the next page you'll see the paragraph that starts about the demographic argument?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see that where says, "the demographic argument helped to understand today's situation. Herzegovinian Croats need to have a reinforcement of Croat population, Herzegovina," et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to give you a fuller opportunity to answer the question that Mr. Praljak put to you in this regard, if you recall, and you weren't really given a chance to give your full answer. Can you comment on the report by -- that's been made in this document and the language that Mr. Praljak had directed to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report, just noting it's Jean-Pierre Thebault's report, the head of the regional centre so I'm commenting on what's written, and we believed that we were seeing the collection of the Croat community into areas of, first of all, immediately safety, and that's when I referred, sir, to your -- to the earlier comment of when there was fighting and when the Croat population was under pressure in places like Travnik and Bugojno, you saw them move literally, as we all imagined, convoys or we've seen on television convoys in the Second World War. People moving out en masse to another area. And there were several things going on. Some were coming into the pockets, and others were going out through the Serb-held territory, which I keep coming back to the cooperation which must have been evident for that to happen. But on top of this is a political overlay as to if there was going to be a third -- sorry, a division of Bosnia into three independent republics, clearly those borders and boundaries would have to be drawn somewhere, and it was always interesting to know what would be acceptable from the Bosnian Croat perspective. And we established and believed, and indeed my discussion with General Praljak suggested that Central Bosnia, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, those were to be inside the boundaries of a republic which may be formed but at the consequence of other Croats who lived further to the north, Zepce, Zavidovici, Tuzla, that they may be -- for them -- for their population to be safe, the best thing to do would be to bring them into secure territory inside of this self-styled republic. And so when we saw movements from Central Bosnia, and particularly from Zepce down from -- from Vares, sorry, down into Herzegovina, it seemed to be a collection of the Croat community beyond that boundary which may or may not be established as an -- one of the three republics. So what's being commented on here by Mr. Thebault is, were some of the Croat population in Central Bosnia -- they were certainly being pushed by the armija forces. I think that's been fairly established -- clearly established. They were being pushed, but was there also another force, a political force on the Croat side that was pulling them into secure areas? I think in Central Bosnia it is very straight forward it's for their protection, but it was movements from Central Bosnia into Herzegovina which, I think, that he's commenting on here, or that he is commenting on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As my last question to you, I believe, sir, can I just direct your attention the next immediately following paragraph, where it says -- where Mr. Thebault says, "It seems Machiavellic, but it is only Balkan. Everybody who has met regularly the top Bosnian Croat leaders (Boban, Stojic, Kordic, Valenta) in various situations and on various subjects, where their paranoia and their extremism were not hidden, can easily believe it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this as well. Now we have this gentleman who I guess is supposed to be a diplomat saying that it is only Balkan. What does that mean? That in and of itself. I think it's a wide pejorative insinuation of the people who live in the Balkans, and the Balkans stretch down to Greece. And I for one am offended by this -- by this comment that somehow the Balkans are a race of people, including the Croats, that somehow they've -- have a particular mind set, and I think that to ask this gentleman to comment on this is wrong and inappropriate, particularly in an international tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honour, I would like to be identified with that, and I would also like to add that it was the same Mr. Scott who about an hour ago objected to Mr. Praljak putting documents to a witness he hadn't seen before with a request to comment on them, and now we're having some hearsay put to this witness who is asked to give pejorative comments about these accused, including my client, when -- when clearly this witness has no basis for doing so, and I join Mr. Karnavas's observation that for the Prosecution to be using this pejorative language is completely out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for, one, Your Honour, I'm not using the language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I will give you the floor, but before the document that we all have before us, the document that was drafted on the 19th of June in 1993, by Ambassador Thebault ... So this document, Mr. Witness, at the time -- had you read this document at the time or are you discovering it today?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document before, sir, yes. I read it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So since you had seen it, you had read it, you can make comments on this document. Now, secondly, regarding the objection made by Mr. Karnavas.
